note: Synthetic memory bank for the concept experiments (2026-09-30). Hand-authored: the concept labels on each memory are the answer key, written with the memory. One memory per turn in the merged shape ('What I experienced: ... What I did: ...'); moods are named start/end states. `about` is what code would tag from engine identity (bodies in the room, a heard speaker).

character.name: Maren Oakes
character.sheet: Maren Oakes, 41, archivist of Hollin's Reach, a river town rebuilt after the flood of 1909. Dry, exact, slow to trust, kind in practical ways. Her younger brother Tomas drowned in the 1909 flood; he knocked on her door that night and she did not open it. Drive: that the record tells the truth, whatever it costs the people in it.

memories.experienced: The archive basement still smelled of river mud. The drying racks were full of warped folios from the flood crates. Jory came down the stairs two at a time with a folded note: the mayor wants the 1909 lock ledger on his desk by Friday, 'for the anniversary display'.
memories.did: I told Jory the ledger was somewhere in the flood crates and that the mayor would have it when I found it. I gave him a biscuit and sent him back up. Then I started on the crates myself, which I had meant to leave until spring. Nobody has asked for the 1909 lock papers in the eleven years I have kept this place, and the mayor has never once asked for anything to display.

memories.experienced: The ledger was in the third crate, wrapped in oilcloth, dry. The pages for the twelfth to the fourteenth of March 1909 were gone. Not torn: cut, close to the spine, with a sharp blade. The stubs were clean and straight.
memories.did: I photographed the stubs under the lamp, three times, with a rule beside them for scale. I wrote the find in the day book with the time. Then I locked the ledger in the map cabinet and put the cabinet key in my coat, not on the hook where it usually hangs. Whoever cut those pages knew exactly which three days to take.

memories.experienced: At the ferry landing a woman in a green coat was asking the ferryman how high the river came in '09. She carried a surveyor's staff and a brass instrument case stamped MINISTRY OF WORKS. The ferryman told her to ask the archive.
memories.did: I bought an eel pie from the stall and ate it slowly, watching her. I did not go over. She measured the height of the old flood mark on the landing post with a tape and wrote it in a green notebook. I went home the long way so I would not pass her.

memories.experienced: At the Anchor, old Hesketh was three glasses gone. When I came in he said, loud enough for the room, 'Your Tomas knew what was coming that night. He had the key.' The room went quiet and then noisy again.
memories.did: I sat down across from him and asked what key. He looked at his glass and said he did not remember saying anything. I asked twice more and he began to cry, so I stopped. I left coins on the table for his next drink and walked home along the towpath past the upper lock, which I have not done in years.

memories.experienced: Tomas's old oilskin coat was still folded in the cedar chest under the window. There was something hard sewn into the lining at the hem. A brass key on a paper tag, the ink faded but readable: UPPER LOCK HOUSE.
memories.did: I sat on the floor with the coat across my knees for a long time. I remembered the knocking that night, and that I lay still and did not go down to open the door because I was angry with him about money. In the end I threaded the key onto a length of string and put it round my neck, under my collar, where nobody would see it.

memories.experienced: Mayor Brine came down to the archive himself at ten, very cordial, hat in hand. He asked whether the ledger had turned up. He said not to worry if it had not, since the fire last winter took most of the lock papers anyway.
memories.did: I told him the ledger had not turned up yet. It was the first lie I have told in this building. I offered him tea, which he refused, and I watched his hands while he talked: he kept turning his hat brim a quarter turn at a time. He did not ask about any other year's papers.

memories.experienced: I took out the fire report from last winter. It says the fire was confined to shelf 14, the lock and sluice papers, and was put out before it spread. It is signed by the mayor's clerk, not by the fire warden.
memories.did: I made a fair copy of the report and noted in the margin that shelf 14 held nothing else of value and that no other shelf was scorched. I checked the warden's own book: he was not called that night. I put the copy with the photographs of the ledger stubs.

memories.experienced: The woman in the green coat came to the archive in the afternoon. She introduced herself as Petra Lusk, surveyor, Ministry of Works, and asked for the levee drawings and whatever flood records we hold. She said the Ministry had received an anonymous letter claiming the levee by the mill was patched with rubble after '09.
memories.did: I brought her the levee drawings and the rainfall tables. I did not mention the ledger. I asked her who wrote the letter and she said she did not know; it was posted from this town. I told her she could work at the long table as long as she liked, and I kept the map cabinet locked while she was there.

memories.experienced: Petra walked the levee with me at dusk. She showed me three seep holes near the mill, water bubbling up through the grass on the dry side. She said the spring melt will be high this year and the patched section may not take it.
memories.did: I told her about the cut ledger pages, the three days in March. I watched her face while I said it and she did not look surprised, only careful. I did not tell her about the key. I said I would find her whatever flood records survived, and I meant it.

memories.experienced: Jory brought a second note: the mayor invites me to dinner tomorrow night. Then, scuffing his boots, Jory said he saw the mayor's clerk burning papers behind the mill last winter, the same week as the archive fire.
memories.did: I gave Jory a coin and told him not to say that to anyone else, not his father, not the ferryman. He promised. I wrote a note accepting the dinner. After he left I wrote down what he had told me, with the date he gave, and put it in the same folder as the fire report.

memories.experienced: Dinner at the mayor's house. A portrait of the old mill owner over the fireplace. Brine talked about the town's recovery and called Tomas 'the hero who tried to open the sluice'. He offered me a seat on the council's heritage board.
memories.did: I drank one glass of wine and declined the board for now. I asked him, as lightly as I could, why the sluice needed opening that night if it was meant to be open in flood. He changed the subject to the new bandstand. Walking out I noticed his study door had a new lock.

memories.experienced: I went to the Upper Lock House on the way home, in the dark. Tomas's key turned in the door. Inside: the logbook shelf was empty, a wall calendar still hung at March 1909, and a crate stamped with the mill company's seal stood under the window.
memories.did: I took the calendar page for March and folded it into my coat. I left the crate where it was because I could not lift it and did not want to scrape it across the floor. I locked the door behind me with the key and stood outside for a while listening to the sluice gates creak.

memories.experienced: At the ferry landing Petra was kneeling beside her level. The bubble vial had been cracked overnight while her instruments were locked in the ferry shed. She said it was deliberate; the case had been forced.
memories.did: I fetched the archive's old levelling rod and a spirit level from the store and helped her recalibrate against the benchmark on the landing post. While we worked I told her about the lock house, the calendar and the mill crate. She asked to see the calendar page and I said tomorrow.

memories.experienced: Hesketh was sober at the lock gate at noon. He told it straight: in 1909 the mill manager ordered the upper sluice held shut to keep the mill wheel pit dry. The water backed up behind the town. Tomas took the lock-house key to open the sluice himself and never came back.
memories.did: I wrote down every word he said in the day book, and read it back to him, and he nodded at each line. Then I asked who carried the order to the lock house. He said, 'Young Brine. He was the mill's clerk then.' I asked him to sign the page and he did, with a shaking hand.

memories.experienced: Alone in the archive I laid the calendar page beside the photographs of the ledger stubs. On the thirteenth of March someone had written in pencil: 'sluice held -- A.B.'
memories.did: I made a fair copy of the calendar and locked both originals in the map cabinet with the ledger. Then I sat at the long table and cried, briefly, for the first time in years, because Tomas went out to open a gate someone had ordered shut, and I would not even open my door to him.

memories.experienced: Jory came in to say the mayor's clerk had been asking him which people visit the archive and how often. Jory had told him only 'the surveyor lady'.
memories.did: I told Jory to stop running errands for the mayor's house for a while and gave him half a loaf and the price of a week's errands so his father would not ask. I told him if anyone asks again he knows nothing about the archive. He looked frightened, then pleased to be trusted.

memories.experienced: Heavy rain all night. The river rose past the landing steps. A note from Petra, delivered wet: 'The levee section by the mill will fail above the eight-foot mark. Tell the council today.'
memories.did: I walked to the river gauge by the mill and read it myself: six feet two inches, and rising. I copied Petra's note in a clear hand and pinned it to the council notice board outside the town hall, and signed my name under hers so it could not be taken for a crank's.

memories.experienced: Council meeting. The mayor called Petra's report 'capital fearmongering' and the council voted to wait and see. Nobody looked at the window, where the rain was coming sideways.
memories.did: I stood up and said the levee failed once before, in 1909, because a sluice was held shut, and that I could prove it. The room went silent. The mayor stared at me and I stared back. I sat down without saying his name, and I have been asking myself since whether that was cowardice or sense.

memories.experienced: After the council Petra found me on the steps and thanked me. Over coffee she said she lost family in a flood in the east when she was a girl, and that guilt keeps records honest if you do not let it rot.
memories.did: I told her about Tomas knocking on my door that night and my lying still. I have never told anyone. She did not say it was not my fault, which I was grateful for. She said, 'Then keep the record,' and paid for the coffee.

memories.experienced: The mayor caught me alone on the archive stairs. Quietly, pleasantly, he said, 'Some doors are best left shut, Maren. Tomas would understand.'
memories.did: I said nothing at all. I held the key under my collar through the cloth until he went up the stairs. Then I went straight to the map cabinet: the lock had fresh scratches around the keyhole but it had held, and everything inside was where I had left it.

memories.experienced: The gauge read seven feet five inches by afternoon. Hesketh and Jory turned up at the mill bank with shovels. Other people came when they saw them.
memories.did: I ran the sandbag line from a list: the 1909 volunteer roll from the archive, the families who dug last time, and I sent Jory to knock on their doors. By dark we had a wall of bags along the weak section. Hesketh worked without a drink all day.

memories.experienced: Night at the Upper Lock House with Petra. The sluice wheel was chained with a new padlock bearing the mill company's mark. Petra said if the sluice stayed shut the water would keep backing onto the patched section.
memories.did: Petra sketched the mechanism by lantern light. I tried Tomas's key on the old iron release box beside the wheel, on an impulse, and it turned: the box held the manual release for the gate, below the chain. We looked at each other for a long moment without speaking.

memories.experienced: We decided to open the sluice partway to take the pressure off the levee. The water ran down the old spillway, loud in the dark. Within an hour Petra's lantern showed the river dropping on the gauge post.
memories.did: I turned the release wheel with Petra, both of us leaning on it. While it turned I thought: this is the door I did not open, and now I am opening it. I did not say it aloud. When it was done I sat on the lock wall and shook until Petra put her coat round me.

memories.experienced: Morning. The levee held; the gauge read seven feet and falling. People cheered at the ferry landing. The mayor stood on a crate and claimed the credit for 'swift emergency measures ordered overnight'.
memories.did: I said nothing in public. Jory caught my eye across the crowd and grinned, and I shook my head at him very slightly, and he understood. I went home and slept until noon for the first time in a week.

memories.experienced: I wrote the whole account of 1909: the ledger stubs, the fire report, the calendar page with its pencilled initials, Hesketh's signed testimony, Jory's account of the burning.
memories.did: I filed one copy in the archive under the flood of 1909, where anyone may read it. I gave the second copy, and the ledger itself, to Petra to carry to the Ministry, because the archive's cabinet is no longer safe and hers is. She promised to hand it to the inquiry office in person.

memories.experienced: Petra left on the morning ferry. She gave me back the archive's levelling rod, and her Ministry card with an address in the capital written on the back.
memories.did: I waved from the landing until the ferry rounded the bend. I put her card in the day book at the page where I had written Hesketh's testimony, so I would find both together.

memories.experienced: Hesketh was asleep in the archive porch in the cold, sober. When I woke him he said Tomas would have been proud of the sandbags and the sluice.
memories.did: I brought him in, fed him soup on the long table, and gave him Tomas's oilskin coat, since it only sat in the chest and he had none. He put it on and did not say anything for a long time.

memories.experienced: A letter from the Ministry: an inquiry is opened into the 1909 flood and the conduct of the mill company. Petra's signature is on the covering note.
memories.did: I read it twice at the long table. Then I walked up to the upper lock and sat on the wall where I had sat that night after the sluice, and watched the water go over the spillway until it was dark.

memories.experienced: Jory ran in with the news: the mayor has resigned 'for reasons of health'. The town is talking of nothing else.
memories.did: I waited to feel something large and did not. I thanked Jory and went back to sorting the flood crates, which I finished that afternoon, eleven years late.

memories.experienced: The anniversary of the flood of 1909. Evening at the Upper Lock House, the door open, the hook by the door empty where a key once hung.
memories.did: I took the brass key off the string round my neck and hung it back on its hook. I said Tomas's name out loud in that room, once, and then I left the door unlocked behind me.

claims.claim: The 1909 flood was a natural disaster nobody could have stopped.
The mayor wants the 1909 ledger because it shows something about March 1909.
Someone deliberately cut out the pages for 12-14 March 1909.
The woman in the green coat is a government surveyor.
claims.subject_name: the woman in the green coat

claims.claim: Tomas had the upper lock key the night of the flood.
The archive fire was set to destroy the lock papers.
Brine, as the mill's clerk, carried the order that held the sluice shut in 1909.
The levee by the mill will fail above eight feet.
Hesketh saw what happened at the lock in 1909.
I failed Tomas by not opening the door.
Opening the sluice was a way of finally opening that door; the debt is paid in the only coin left.
